To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increasing input image size and using shallow models can yield competitive performance on a challenging object detection task.

(a) upsampling the image by a factor of 4 offers 12 percentage-points better accuracy than an off-the-shelve baseline, (b) using earlier and shallower layers in a CNN offers higher accuracy than later and deeper layers, (c) using a shallow model with upsampling yields higher accuracy than a deep model without upsampling.

1) increasing input image resolution offers up to 10 percentage-points higher accuracy than the baseline; 2) earlier/shallower models offer higher accuracy than later models; 3) a simple shallow model with upsampled input image offers competitive accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art; 4) our model achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the art on the KITTI benchmark.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
shallow networks can be used to obtain high accuracy in the road object-detection problem.

we find that the most accurate models for road object detection are not the ones with the largest number of parameters or deepest layers, but rather ones that are shallow and use upsampled input images.
we show how a combination of shallow networks and upsampled input images can achieve high-accuracy road object-detection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for high-accuracy detection, we should not be afraid to use more shallow networks or to upsample images.
the accuracy of detection systems can be improved by simple and intuitive modifications to existing architectures.
there is a need to re-evaluate the use of deeper and larger models for object detection tasks.
